notes: The circuit image shows the breadboard with rows f-j at the top and a-e at the bottom, so the catalogue's 'b' bank (f-j) is the upper half and its 't' bank (a-e) is the lower half. The rails next to the lower half are therefore tp/tn, with tp as the + rail and tn as the - rail.

Column numbers and rail hole indices were estimated from pixel positions in the image. The button sits in columns 4 and 6, the resistor in columns 6 and 9, and the rail holes are indexed 1-5 and 6-10 in the two groups.
Button side pairing: 1.l and 1.r are the two legs in column 4 (the 5V side). 2.l and 2.r are the two legs in column 6 (the pin 2 / pull-down side).

Pin 2 connects to the column-6 strip on the upper half, which joins the button leg. The pull-down resistor is on the lower-half column-6 strip, which is joined through the button's side 2. The pull-down resistor therefore sits on the same side as the input pin, as the manual says.
The resistor is a 10k pull-down, so value=10000. No external LED is used, because the sketch drives the built-in LED on pin 13.

The circuit image shows the boards wired directly with the two 4.7 kΩ pull-ups drawn as free resistors. I modelled the pull-ups and the shared SDA/SCL/3V3 nodes on one mini breadboard (bb1) using jumper wires. The manual lists two mini breadboards, but the image doesn't show how the second one is used, so I left it out.
SDA is on A4 and SCL on A5 for both boards, as the manual states. A4 goes to A4 and A5 goes to A5.
Both pull-ups go to the 3.3 V pin of the reader board, labelled '3V' in the image. The Nano 33 IoT is 3.3 V logic and not 5 V tolerant, so 3V3 is the correct supply.
GND goes directly between the two boards by one jumper wire.
Both boards are powered and programmed over USB from the computer. The computer is not modelled as a part, so the USB cables have only the board-side edge.
The built-in LED of the reader board is not a separate part. The 3V3 pin of the writer is not connected.

The manual's wiring images are not provided (only a generic 'rpi-gpio-wiring-a-button' include and a video), so the layout is the standard one: each tactile switch straddles the breadboard centre gap, with the GPIO pin on the top-half side and ground on the bottom-half side.
Pins GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27 and GPIO10 come from the full code listing. The manual says any GPIO pins can be used.

The catalogue card for raspberry-pi-4 lists only a single GPIO_HEADER port. Following the task instructions, I used individual header pin names (GPIO4, GPIO17, GPIO27, GPIO10, GND) as ports on the board. They may need to be added to the card.

Pushbutton orientation is an assumption: side 1 (1.l, 1.r) goes in the top half and side 2 (2.l, 2.r) in the bottom half. The button is wired GPIO to ground (gpiozero Button uses the internal pull-up), so no external resistor is needed.

Each of the four buttons uses its own column pair on the breadboard (3-5, 8-10, 13-15, 18-20). The bottom-half strip of each button links to the bottom negative rail (bn) with a pin-to-pin jumper. A pin-to-socket jumper joins one Pi GND pin to that rail.
For the male-to-female jumpers, the 'a' end is the female socket on the Pi pin and the 'b' end is the male pin in the breadboard.
The Pi has five pin-to-socket leads (4 GPIO + 1 GND) and four pin-to-pin leads (one ground link per button), as the manual's parts list says.

Speakers or headphones plug into the Pi's audio output. The catalogue card has no audio-jack port and the manual shows no wiring for it, so they are left out of the graph. The sounds are played in software with pygame.
